docs.title: Triarc Framework
docs.text: This repository contains a general application framework for creating systems with multiple concurrent processes.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Documentation is available here.

docs.text: The most recent version, as well as older versioms, are available as a VI Package under the Release section at GitHub.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
If you are familiar with queued message handler based applications, using the basics of Triarc is quite straight forward.

Reading through the documentation should provide what is needed to get started. As everything is available as open source, it is worth exploring the source to understand how the framework is implemented.

Examples are available at https://github.com/Astemes/astemes-triarc-examples

docs.text: The debugger is a useful tool which is available here: https://github.com/Astemes/astemes-triarc-debugger

docs.title: Introduction to Triarc Framework
docs.text: This page gives a short introduction to the Triarc Framework (TF) and an overview of its main ideas. The framework is developed and maintained by Astemes and is released under an open source license.

docs.title: What is Triarc Framework
docs.text:
Triarc is an application framework for building concurrent applications in LabVIEW. It provides three core abstractions: Processes, Applications, and Views. You extend these classes to build your own applications.

The framework manages the lifecycle of every process and the communication channels between processes. It also provides the boilerplate for error handling, logging and configuration management.

The API of a TF process looks like the API of an instrument driver, so it should feel familiar to any LabVIEW developer. In the example below, the process is initialized and started before the while loop, used through its API inside the loop, and stopped and cleared after the loop.

TF is based on the actor model, a proven way of managing concurrent and distributed processing. The design goal is to give you the benefits of an actor based system, with a simple API and without unnecessary complexity.

The framework is developed test first. Modules built on TF are testable, and they can be designed to follow the SOLID principles.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Concept In short Read more Process An actor: a class with private state and a message loop managed by the framework. Process Application A process that owns other processes and manages their lifecycle. Application View A process with a front panel. View Message A string and a variant, sent to a process through an API VI. Messaging Request A message that waits for, or calls back with, a response. Requests Broadcast A one-to-many notification from a process to anyone who registered. Broadcasting Helper Loop A periodic action running in parallel to a process. Helper Loops Async Handler A blocking or slow action running in parallel to a process. Async Handler

docs.title: Why Yet Another Framework?
docs.text:
There are well established frameworks in the LabVIEW ecosystem, most notably NI Actor Framework and DQMH. Each has its own benefits and drawbacks, but neither fitted our needs and workflow well. A test rig architecture grew over a few incarnations, and from it a generic high level framework could be extracted, distilled, tested and improved.

Triarc processes are composable, independent, and testable. The framework encourages modularity and lets you compose applications out of small processes, each with a single responsibility. Communication between processes is robust, and the framework manages the lifecycle of each process. The framework provides entry points for error handling and logging, and a powerful debugger is available.

There may not be a great demand for a new framework, but there was no reason to keep Triarc private or closed. Releasing it as open source enforces proper, publicly available version management. It is valuable for all users of the framework, and anyone can contribute both ideas and code.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page walks through creating a first Triarc process and running it from a top level VI. It assumes that you know the LabVIEW queued message handler pattern and have used LabVIEW classes.

docs.title: Install the Framework
docs.text:
Install the Triarc Framework VI Package with VI Package Manager. The package installs:

  • the framework library TF.lvlib in vi.lib\Astemes\Triarc Framework, with palettes,
  • the Triarc Framework Test Suite (see Testing),
  • IDE integration: menu items under Tools » Triarc and right-click menu items for processes in the project window,
  • the framework error codes (see Error Handling).

docs.title: Create a Process
docs.text:
1. Open or create a LabVIEW project.
  2. Select Tools » Triarc » Add Framework Library to Project to add TF.lvlib to the project.
  3. Select Tools » Triarc » New Triarc Process. In the dialog, select the parent class, enter a name for the process and select the folder to save it in. The parent can be Process, View, Application, or any process class already in the project.
  4. The tool creates the class, overrides Handle Messages.vi and adds the class to the project.

docs.title: Add an API VI
docs.text:
Other code talks to a process only through its API VIs. Right-click the process class in the project window and select:

  • Generate API VI... to create a VI that sends a message to the process. Enter the message name in the dialog. The tool creates the API VI and adds a case for the message to Handle Messages.vi.
  • Generate Getter... to create a VI that reads a field of the private class data through a request.
  • Generate Setter... to create a VI that writes a field of the private class data through a message.

The generated VIs use the dual-mode pattern described in Handling Messages: called from outside the process they send a message, and called from inside the process loop they do the work.

Implement the behavior in the case of Handle Messages.vi that handles the message. The Handle Messages.vi is the only place where the class data may be unbundled and bundled. Keep the Default case calling the parent method, so that messages defined by the parent classes are still handled.

docs.title: Run the Process
docs.text:
A top level VI uses a process like an instrument driver:

  1. Create the process object (a class constant) and call Init.vi with a name.
  2. Optionally configure an error handler with Set Error Handler.vi and log handlers with Add Log Handler.vi.
  3. Call Start.vi. The VI returns when the process is running.
  4. Call the API VIs of the process.
  5. Call Stop.vi. The VI returns when the process has finished.
  6. Call Clear.vi to release the resources allocated by Init.vi.

For an application with more than one process, create an Application, initialize each process, and add it with Add Process.vi. The application then starts, stops and clears its processes for you. See Application.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Read Process to learn the process lifecycle.
  • Read Best Practices before the application grows.
  • Look at the examples in astemes-triarc-examples.
  • If you use an AI coding agent, point it at the Agent Guide.

docs.title: Framework Architecture
docs.text: This page describes the core classes and interfaces of the Triarc Framework (TF) and how they depend on each other. The hierarchy is shown below.

docs.title: Framework Classes
docs.text:
The framework classes are the starting point for every Triarc module. They manage the lifecycle of the processes in an application and let you compose processes into larger modules.

Base                    Name and configuration file scaffolding
└── Process             Message loop and lifecycle (implements Error Handler Interface and Logging)
    ├── View            Adds a front panel, View.vi
    └── Application     Owns other processes (implements Async Handler)
Class Responsibility Read more Base Holds the name of the object and the configuration file path and reference. Can be used on its own for components that do not run asynchronously. Base Process Runs a message loop, manages the lifecycle, and provides messaging, requests, broadcasts, error handling and logging. Process View A Process with a user interface in View.vi. View Application A Process that owns other processes and applies lifecycle, error handlers and log handlers to them. Application

Note that Application inherits from Process, not from View. An application has no panel of its own. Add views to it to give it a user interface.

docs.title: Framework Interfaces
docs.text:
The framework interfaces decorate a class with additional behavior. For example, a class that implements the Configuration File interface can read and write its own section of a configuration file through the API of the interface.

Interface What it adds Read more Helper Loop Helper Action.vi, run periodically in parallel to the process. Helper Loops Async Handler Async Action.vi, run once in parallel to the process for slow or blocking work. Async Handler Configuration Storage-agnostic API for reading and writing configuration values. Configuration Configuration File Implementation of Configuration that stores values in an ini file. Configuration Error Handler Interface Handle Errors.vi. Implement it to create an error handler. Every Process implements it and delegates to its configured error handler. Error Handling Logging Log Debug.vi … Log Critical.vi, and the Log.vi method that a log handler overrides. Every Process implements it and delegates to its configured log handlers. Logging Callback Callback.vi, called when the response to an asynchronous request arrives. Requests

A class lists only its direct parent and the interfaces it declares itself. To find everything a class can do, follow its ancestors: a View is also a Process, an Error Handler Interface, a Logging and a Base.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text: All framework classes are members of TF.lvlib. The library also contains Broadcast Event Helpers.lvlib, with VIs for dequeuing broadcast events outside an event structure. These VIs are deprecated in TF.lvlib and will be removed from it in a future release. A one-to-one replacement is installed in the support directory of the framework.

docs.title: Base
docs.text: The Base class is the common ancestor of all Triarc processes. It can also be used on its own, for components that do not run asynchronously but should be named and configurable in the same way as processes.

docs.title: Name
docs.text:
Base stores the name of the object. The name is set by Init.vi and cannot be changed afterwards. If no name is given, the name of the class is used.

The name should be unique among the processes owned by the same application. Processes in different applications may have the same name, because a process is identified by its qualified name, which includes the names of its owners (see Application).

VI Returns Read Base Name.vi The name given at initialization. Read Name.vi (on Process) The name and the qualified name, Owner::Name, built from the chain of owning applications.

docs.title: Configuration Scaffolding
docs.text:
Base holds the data that the Configuration File interface needs: the path to the configuration file and the reference to the open file. A class that should be configurable inherits this scaffolding from Base and implements the Configuration File interface. See Configuration.

The configuration file path is an optional input of Init.vi. If it is not wired, the default path is used. Read Config File Path.vi returns the path in use.

docs.title: Init and Clear
docs.text: Init.vi initializes the object and creates any references it needs. Clear.vi releases everything created by Init.vi. Both are dynamic dispatch VIs. Descendants that override them must call the parent method.

docs.title: Process
docs.text: The Process is the fundamental building block of a Triarc application, similar to an actor in Actor Framework or a module in DQMH. A process is a class. Its private data is the state of the process, and the framework runs a message loop that owns this state.

docs.title: Process Lifecycle
docs.text:
The framework keeps track of the lifecycle state of each process. The lifecycle state is a core concept that the framework uses to keep itself consistent, for example to refuse a request to a process that is not running. The normal evolution of the lifecycle is shown below.

State Meaning Uninitialized The process object has been created but Init.vi has not been called. Initialized Init.vi has been called. Messages can be sent, but they are not handled until the process is started. Started Start.vi has launched the process loop, which has not yet handled the Start message. Running The process loop has handled the Start message and is handling messages. Stopped Stop.vi has been called. Messages already in the queue are still handled. Finished The process loop has handled the Stop message and exited. The process can be started again or cleared.

A process always starts as Uninitialized and moves to Initialized when Init.vi is called. Init.vi is a dynamic dispatch method. Override it to allocate resources and open references used by the process. Do not configure hardware or start other processes in Init.vi. Do that when the process starts.

When the process is started, the process loop is launched asynchronously. Start.vi waits until the process has handled the Start message and reached the Running state, or until the timeout expires.

The process then lives its own life in the process loop until it is stopped with Stop.vi. Stop.vi sends a Stop message and waits until the process loop has finished, or until the timeout expires. The process object returned by Stop.vi contains the state of the process as it was when the loop finished.

A finished process can be restarted with Start.vi, or cleared with Clear.vi to release the resources allocated in Init.vi. Restarting a process is a supported use case.

The framework checks the lifecycle state and returns an error when a method is called in the wrong state:

Situation Error Start.vi, Stop.vi and most other methods called on an uninitialized process 9500, Process not initialized Init.vi called on an initialized process 9511, Process already initialized Start.vi called on a running process 9514, Trying to start process which is already running Clear.vi called on a running process 9504, Process cleared while running

See Error Handling for all framework error codes.

docs.title: Reading and Waiting for the Lifecycle State
docs.text:
Get Lifecycle State.vi returns the current lifecycle state. Wait for Life Cycle State.vi waits until the process reaches a given state, or until the timeout expires.

Every change of lifecycle state is also broadcast with the message Lifecycle, so other processes and views can follow it. See Broadcasting.

docs.title: The Process Loop
docs.text:
When a Process is started, the process loop is launched asynchronously. Each process keeps its own state in the process loop. A very important principle is that the state may only be accessed from within the process loop. There is no limit on the number of processes running at the same time, and many processes of the same class may run in parallel.

The process loop is essentially a queued message handler. It receives the messages enqueued by API VIs and passes each of them to Handle Messages.vi. The VI running the loop is private to the framework. To add functionality to a process, you override Handle Messages.vi.

The framework adds debugging, logging and error handling to the process loop. An error returned by Handle Messages.vi is passed to the error handler of the process, with the qualified name of the process and the message as location.

docs.title: The Handle Messages.vi
docs.text:
To make a process do something useful, override Handle Messages.vi. The VI is called in the process loop for every message received, and you define the behavior by adding cases to its case structure. The process data should only be accessed in Handle Messages.vi, which makes it safe to read and update the data without race conditions.

The Default case should always call Call Parent Class Method to pass unhandled messages to the parent. This keeps the message handler free of repetition: only the specific responsibility of the process is in its message handler. As the number of cases in a Handle Messages.vi is usually small, it is easy to read.

The Process class itself handles the messages Init, Start, Stop, Trigger Broadcast, Set Error Handler and Add Log Handler. A message that no class in the hierarchy handles causes error 9503, Unknown command received.

You can add behavior to a framework message by adding its case to your Handle Messages.vi and calling the parent method from that case. For Start, call the parent method last: the parent sets the Running state, which releases the Start.vi that is waiting. For Stop, do your clean-up (for example disconnecting hardware) and then call the parent method. The parent always stops the process, even if an error is wired to it.

See Handling Messages for how to write API VIs and message cases.

docs.title: The Read Configuration.vi
docs.text:
Configuration management is a central issue for most test systems, so it is part of the framework. Read Configuration.vi is a protected dynamic dispatch VI that you can override to load the configuration of the process. The framework calls it from the process loop when it handles the Init message, which is the first message handled when the process starts.

Set the configured values directly in the class data in Read Configuration.vi. Do not send messages to the process from it: other messages may already be queued and would then be handled before the configuration has been loaded. See Configuration.

docs.title: Process Context
docs.text:
When a process is added to an application, the process knows its context. If process A is added to application B, then B is the context of A. If application B is in turn added to application C, the context of A is still B, and the context of B is C. If C is the top level application, it has no context.

Get Context.vi returns the context of a process, and a Top Level? flag that is true when the process has no context. Tracking the context lets a process communicate back to its owner. To do that in a useful way, the process makes some assertions about the context it runs in, for example that the context implements a given interface.

The context is also used to build the qualified name of the process, and to find an error handler or log handler when the process has none of its own.

docs.title: Inside or Outside the Process Loop
docs.text:
The same process object can be used both inside the process loop, in Handle Messages.vi, and outside it, in the code that calls the API. Get Lifecycle State.vi returns an API Mode that tells the two apart:

API Mode Meaning Send Message The VI is called from outside the process loop. It should send a message to the process. Handle Message The VI is called from inside the process loop. It should do the work directly and must not send messages to its own process.

Some framework methods are only allowed in one of the modes. Launch Helper Loop.vi, Launch Async Handler.vi and Stop Helper Loops.vi must be called from inside the process loop (error 9509). Request Message.vi must not be called from inside the process loop of the process it requests from, because it would wait for itself (error 9507).

The API Mode is carried by value on the process wire. If you branch the process wire inside the process loop and pass the branch to code that runs outside the loop, call Leave Process Loop.vi on the branch first. Get Lifecycle State.vi then returns Send Message for that branch, so API VIs called on it send messages instead of touching the process data. Helper loops do this for you.

docs.title: Application
docs.text: A program is usually made of many small processes, each handling one responsibility of the application. In Triarc, processes are composed into applications.

docs.title: The Triarc Application
docs.text:
The Application class inherits from the Process class. Its purpose is to manage the lifecycle of other processes. The Application has the API shown below, and it also inherits the API of the Process.

VI Description Add Process.vi Adds an initialized process to the application. The application then owns the process and manages its lifecycle. Get Process.vi Returns an owned process by name. Accepts qualified names for processes in nested applications. Get All Processes.vi Returns all processes owned by the application. Remove Process.vi Removes a process from the application and returns it, without stopping or clearing it. Shutdown Process.vi Stops and clears a process and removes it from the application. Register for Broadcasting Events Recursively.vi Registers for the broadcasts of the application and all processes in it, including nested applications.

Each process can reach its owning application with Get Context.vi.

As the Application is itself a Process, applications can be nested. This lets you build rich architectures with layers of subsystems.

docs.title: Adding Processes
docs.text:
Initialize a process with Init.vi before adding it with Add Process.vi. Adding an uninitialized process returns error 9500, and adding a process with the same name as one already in the application returns a duplicate item error.

After a process has been added, the application owns its lifecycle. You do not need to start, stop or clear processes that are owned by an application.

A common place to add processes is the Read Configuration.vi of the application, where the names and the number of processes can be read from the configuration file.

docs.title: Getting Processes
docs.text:
Get Process.vi returns an owned process by name, as a Process. Cast it to the expected class to call its API.

A good pattern is to wrap Get Process.vi in a VI that hard codes the name of the process and casts the result to the expected class. The name and the class are then defined in one place only, which makes them easy to change.

If the process name refers to the application itself, the application is returned.

docs.title: Qualified Names
docs.text:
Every process has a qualified name: the names of its owners and its own name, joined with ::. For example, a process Source in an application Motion that is owned by the top level application Main has the qualified name Main::Motion::Source.

To get a process in a nested application, pass its qualified name to Get Process.vi. If no process with the name is found, Get Process.vi returns error 9512, Could not find requested process.

The qualified name is also used as the location for errors, as the source of log entries, as the window title of views, and as the name of the configuration section of the process.

docs.title: Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
An application is responsible for the processes it owns, and they follow its lifecycle. When the application is started or stopped, all its owned processes are started or stopped too. When the application is cleared, all its owned processes are cleared.

Processes added while the application is running are not started automatically. This lets you add idle processes to a running application and start them when they are needed.

To remove a process from a running application, use Shutdown Process.vi, which stops, clears and removes the process. Remove Process.vi only removes the process. You are then responsible for its lifecycle.

The application broadcasts Process Added and Process Removed when processes are added and removed.

docs.title: Recursion through the Application
docs.text:
Some operations on an Application are applied recursively to the processes it owns, and to the processes in nested applications:

  • lifecycle operations (start, stop, clear),
  • Set Error Handler.vi, which configures the error handler for all owned processes,
  • Add Log Handler.vi, which adds the log handler to all owned processes,
  • Register for Broadcasting Events Recursively.vi.

Error handlers and log handlers also apply to processes that are added to the application after the handler was configured. It is therefore enough to configure them once, on the top level application.

docs.title: View
docs.text: A Triarc Process is headless: it runs without a user interface. Indicators may be added to Handle Messages.vi for debugging, but this is not a good way to build a user interface. The View class, which inherits from Process, adds a user interface to the process. Use it to build user interface components. Complex user interfaces are usually composed of many small views inserted into subpanels.

docs.title: Anatomy of a View
docs.text:
The View class adds a VI called View.vi, and methods for showing and hiding its front panel. The API also has a method that returns a reference to the running View.vi, which can be used to insert the view into a subpanel. The API is shown below.

VI Description View.vi The user interface. Protected and dynamic dispatch: override it in your view class. Show Panel.vi Opens the front panel of the running View.vi. Hide Panel.vi Closes the front panel. View.vi keeps running. Get View VI Reference.vi Returns the reference to the running View.vi, for example to insert it into a subpanel. Set View VI Reference.vi Protected. Called by View.vi when it starts, to report its reference to the framework.

The framework launches View.vi when the view process starts and sets the window title to the qualified name of the process. Show Panel.vi returns error 9506 if the view is not running. When the panel is shown or hidden, the view broadcasts a View Panel message.

docs.title: Requirements on the View.vi
docs.text:
The framework asserts two requirements on View.vi, and it is important that both are met:

  1. When it starts, View.vi reports a reference to itself with Set View VI Reference.vi.
  2. View.vi stops when the Stop message is broadcast.

This is shown below. A unit test that checks both requirements is created with the class when the class is created with Tools » Triarc » New Triarc Process.

A typical View.vi:

  • registers for the broadcasts of its own process with Register for Broadcast Events.vi,
  • calls Set View VI Reference.vi with a reference to This VI,
  • runs an event structure that handles user interface events and broadcast events,
  • exits its loop when the Stop broadcast is received,
  • handles Panel Close? by calling Hide Panel.vi and discarding the event, so that closing the window hides the panel instead of stopping the view.

docs.title: Communicating between the Process and the View
docs.text:
View.vi and Handle Messages.vi run concurrently, in separate VIs, with some given communication channels.

When the user interacts with the view, View.vi may call any API method of the process to send messages to the process loop. As View.vi belongs to the process class, these API VIs may even be private.

Communication from Handle Messages.vi in the process loop to View.vi is usually done with broadcasts. The process loop broadcasts a message, and View.vi handles it to update the user interface.

Another way to update the user interface is to send references to indicators from View.vi to the process, and update the indicators with property nodes in Handle Messages.vi.

Remember that View.vi runs outside the process loop. It must not unbundle or bundle the class data. Use API VIs to change the state of the process.

docs.title: Handling Messages
docs.text: Users of a process send messages to it by calling API VIs on the process wire. The users are not necessarily human. All messages are enqueued with the same priority to the process loop, where they are received and passed to Handle Messages.vi. This VI is the core of every process.

docs.title: The Handle Messages.vi
docs.text:
Handle Messages.vi is called in the process loop and receives every message sent to the process through the API. Think of it as a subVI that contains only the case structure of a traditional LabVIEW queued message handler. As shown below, Handle Messages.vi receives the message string and the message data variant, and has access to the process wire.

A very important rule in Triarc is that Handle Messages.vi is the only place where the data on the class wire is accessible and valid. In other words, this is the only place where the class wire may be unbundled or bundled.

Each case should:

  1. convert Message Data to the expected type with Variant To Data,
  2. do the work, typically by calling the API VI that sent the message, or a subVI with the core logic,
  3. if the message was a request, call Response Message.vi on every path, including when an error occurred, or launch an async action that responds (see Requests).

Each message should be handled atomically, in one case. Avoid sending messages from Handle Messages.vi to the process itself: other messages may be handled in between. Use process state and a Helper Loop for repeated or multi-step behavior.

docs.title: API VIs
docs.text:
The messaging VIs (Send Message.vi, Request Message.vi, …) are protected. Every message therefore needs a public (or private) API VI in the class that handles it. The API VI hard codes the message string and has typed inputs and outputs for the message data.

The API VIs created by the Triarc tools (Generate API VI..., Generate Getter... and Generate Setter... in the right-click menu of a process class) are dual-mode VIs. They call Get Lifecycle State.vi and switch on its API Mode output:

API Mode Called from The API VI Send Message Outside the process: another process, a view, a test, a top level VI. Sends the message with Send Message.vi, or makes a request with Request Message.vi and returns the response. Handle Message Inside the process loop, from Handle Messages.vi. Does the work on the class data.

The case in Handle Messages.vi that handles the message calls the same API VI, which now runs in Handle Message mode. The behavior of the message is then defined in one VI, and the message string appears in exactly two places: the API VI and the case name.

When you rename a message, change both the string constant in the API VI and the case name in Handle Messages.vi. The type converted with Variant To Data in the case must match the type the API VI sends.

docs.title: Overriding Messages
docs.text:
Since every message is passed to Handle Messages.vi, it also receives the messages defined by API VIs of the parent classes. The normal behavior is to call Call Parent Class Method in the Default case and let the parent handle the message.

You can also handle a parent message in a child class, to replace or extend the behavior of the parent. To extend it, handle the message and call the parent method from the same case. This is an example of how a Triarc process follows the open-closed principle.

Messages handled by the framework classes:

Class Messages Process Init, Start, Stop, Trigger Broadcast, Set Error Handler, Add Log Handler View Start, Stop, Show Panel, Hide Panel, Get View VI Reference Application Start, Stop, Trigger Broadcast, Set Error Handler, Add Log Handler, Add Process, Get Process, Get All Processes, Remove Process, Shutdown Process

A message that no class handles ends up in the Default case of Process, which returns error 9503, Unknown command received.

docs.title: Messaging
docs.text: The main communication channel in Triarc is passing messages to a process.

docs.title: The Messaging API
docs.text:
The messaging API is small, as seen below.

VI Description Send Message.vi Enqueues a message to the process. Returns immediately. Request Message.vi Enqueues a request and waits for the response. See Requests. Async Request Message.vi Enqueues a request. The response is delivered to a Callback. See Requests. Response Message.vi Sends the response to a request, from the case that handles the request or from an async action launched from that case. Enqueue Message.vi Deprecated. Use Send Message.vi.

All these VIs are protected, so they can only be called from the class and its descendants. A message is a string, Message, and a variant, Message Data.

There are no priority levels, and messages are handled in the order they are sent. The VI that receives messages is private to the Process class and is only used in the process loop.

docs.title: Sending Messages
docs.text:
A message is sent to the process with Send Message.vi, and it is received in Handle Messages.vi of the process. When it receives a message, the process may run some logic, change its state data, launch new processes, broadcast a message, and so on.

Handle each message atomically, implementing the full functionality in one case of Handle Messages.vi. There is no guarantee that other messages are not handled in between if one API call sends several messages.

docs.title: Messaging through the Lifecycle
docs.text:
Messages may be sent both while a process is running and before it has been started. Messages sent before the process is started are not handled until it is started.

When the process starts, the first message handled is always the framework's Init message. Then all messages sent before the process was started are handled, and then the Start message.

Stop.vi sends a Stop message. Messages sent after Stop.vi was called, but before the Stop message is handled, are handled before the process finishes. This allows a controlled and clean stop. If a process must be terminated quickly, Clear.vi terminates it immediately.

Messages can still be sent to a stopped process, but they are not handled unless the process is started again. Restarting a process is fully supported.

docs.title: Type Safety
docs.text:
The messages of a process are defined by the class that handles them. Since the messaging VIs are protected, each message needs an API VI that enqueues it. The API VI should hard code the message string and enforce the data type of the message data. This protects against misspelled message strings and makes sure the expected data type is sent. It also gives the process a clear, robust high level API, which helps both testing and readability.

See Handling Messages for the API VI pattern.

docs.title: Broadcasting
docs.text: Broadcasting is a communication channel for one-to-many messages. A process broadcasts a message without knowing who, if anyone, receives it. This keeps the sender decoupled from the receivers.

docs.title: Implementation using User Events
docs.text:
Broadcasts are sent as User Events with a fixed data type, the Broadcast Message Cluster:

Element Content Sender The name of the process that sent the broadcast. Message The broadcast message string. Message Data A variant with the data of the broadcast.

The framework creates the User Event and manages the event registration.

docs.title: Sending Broadcasts
docs.text:
A process sends a broadcast with the protected Broadcast Message.vi. As with messages, wrap it in a VI that hard codes the message string and the data type, so that senders and receivers agree on both.

Since the data is a variant, each receiver must know which type to expect for a given message. Document the message names and data types of the broadcasts of a process.

docs.title: Receiving Broadcasts
docs.text:
To register for the broadcasts of a process, use Register for Broadcast Events.vi. To register for the broadcasts of an Application and all processes in it, including nested applications, use Register for Broadcasting Events Recursively.vi.

Handle the broadcasts in an event structure, as shown above. Switch on Message in the user event case, and convert Message Data to the expected type. Use Sender to tell processes apart when you are registered for broadcasts from more than one process.

Get Broadcast Event.vi returns the User Event itself, for code that needs to build its own event registration.

docs.title: Trigger Broadcast
docs.text:
Trigger Broadcast.vi sends the Trigger Broadcast message to a process. Override the Trigger Broadcast case in Handle Messages.vi to broadcast the current state of the process, and call the parent method from the case so that the parent classes can broadcast their state too.

A new view, or any other new observer, can then call Trigger Broadcast.vi after registering, to receive the current state instead of waiting for the next change. For an application, Trigger Broadcast is forwarded to all owned processes.

docs.title: Framework Broadcasts
docs.text:
The framework broadcasts the following messages:

Message Sent by When Lifecycle Every process On every lifecycle change. The data identifies the new state, for example Running, Finished or Cleared. Stop View When the view is stopped. Every View.vi must exit when it receives this broadcast. View Panel View When the front panel is shown or hidden. Process Added, Process Removed Application When a process is added to or removed from the application. Helper Loop Processes with helper loops When a helper loop starts, runs and stops. Async Handler Processes with async handlers When an async handler starts, runs and finishes.

Do not use these message names for your own broadcasts.

docs.title: Debugging Broadcasts
docs.text: With the DEBUG conditional disable symbol set to TRUE, every broadcast is logged at the debug level. The debugger can also show broadcasts.

docs.title: Requests and Responses
docs.text: A Triarc application consists of processes that run independently and communicate by exchanging messages. Broadcasts can be used to publish the result of handling a message. In addition, the request message type can be used for blocking and non-blocking requests, as described below.

docs.title: Synchronous Requests and Responses
docs.text:
Sometimes it is useful to make a synchronous request to a process. When something should be returned from the process to the sender of a message, use Request Message.vi. The process that receives the request must call Response Message.vi to return a response to the requester. Response Message.vi is called from the case in Handle Messages.vi that handles this specific message, as shown below, or from an async action launched from that case (see Responding from an Async Handler).

A request is a serialized operation: Request Message.vi blocks until a response is returned or the timeout expires. If a request is made from another process, that process is stuck waiting for the response and cannot handle any other message while it waits. This introduces a risk of deadlocks and other quirks of concurrent systems, so use requests with care.

The Triarc request-response pattern keeps coupling low, because the request and the response are implemented entirely in the responding class, which exposes the request API VI. Changing the implementation only requires changes to the responding class, as long as the returned data type stays the same. If the type has to change, the API VI changes, which gives a compile-time error in the callers instead of a hidden bug.

docs.title: Rules for Requests
docs.text:
• Respond on every path. The case handling a request must call Response Message.vi also when an error occurred. Otherwise the requester waits until its timeout expires.
  • Respond exactly once. The requester keeps only one response. A second response sent before the first is read replaces it.
  • Pass errors back. An error wired into Response Message.vi is returned to the requester as error 9515, The Request caused an error in the process.
  • Choose a timeout longer than the work. The default timeout, -1, waits forever. Use a finite timeout for anything that talks to hardware or the network.
  • Do not request from yourself. A request from inside the process loop to the same process would wait for itself. It returns error 9507.
  • Only request from running processes. A request to a process that is not started or running returns error 9506.
Error Meaning 9502 The process was stopped while the request was waiting. 9505 The request timed out. Timed out? is also true. 9506 The process is not running. 9507 Request to self from inside the process loop. 9510 The response could not be delivered, for example because the request had already timed out. 9515 The process returned an error with the response.

docs.title: Responding from an Async Handler
docs.text:
Some requests take a long time to handle, for example a move that waits for hardware. Handling them in the case would block the process loop, so the process could not handle other messages, such as a stop, until the request is done.

Instead, the case that receives the request can start the work and launch an Async Handler, and the async action calls Response Message.vi when the work is done. The requester waits as usual, but the process loop is free to handle other messages in the meantime.

  • The response is carried by the class data that is passed to Launch Async Handler.vi, so launch the action from the case that receives the request.
  • The action can respond at any time, also after the process has handled other messages, and also after Leave Process Loop.vi has been called on the class data.
  • The case must not respond when it has launched an action that responds. The action must respond on every path, including errors and cancellation.
  • If the case decides not to launch the action, for example because the request is rejected, it responds itself.
  • Choose the requester's timeout to cover the whole operation, not only the time in the case.

A helper loop cannot respond to a request, because it is not launched from the case that receives the request.

docs.title: Asynchronous Requests
docs.text:
In some cases a synchronous request is acceptable or even desirable, but in many situations a blocking wait for a response is not. The recommended way to solve this in Triarc is Async Request Message.vi, introduced in version 1.0.24.

In addition to the Message string and the Message Data variant, Async Request Message.vi takes a Callback. Callback is an interface with one method, Callback.vi, which receives the response message and data. When the receiving process calls Response Message.vi, the Callback.vi of the object passed to Async Request Message.vi is called.

This is a very powerful way to implement requests, as it does not couple the callee directly to the caller. There is an indirect coupling, though: if the data or formatting of the response changes, it may break the function of the caller.

A common implementation is to let the requesting process implement Callback, and have its Callback.vi send the response to the requesting process as a message. Callback.vi is called by Response Message.vi, so it runs in the process loop of the responding process. It should return quickly, and it must not access the data of the requesting process directly. If the requesting process passes itself as Callback from inside its own process loop, call Leave Process Loop.vi on the object first, so that API VIs called on it in Callback.vi send messages.

Request Message.vi is itself built on Async Request Message.vi, with the Synchronous Request Callback class waiting for the response.

docs.title: Asynchronous Requests prior to Version 1.0.24
docs.text:
Before Async Request Message.vi existed, asynchronous requests were made from an Async Handler. This still works and is sometimes useful. The request API VI is called in Async Action.vi, and Launch Async Handler.vi is called when the request needs to be dispatched. The request then runs asynchronously to the process, and the same process can even dispatch several concurrent requests and wait for their responses.

When the response returns, it is received in Async Action.vi, which can forward it to the process as a regular message. Note that the async action runs outside the process loop and cannot change the state of the process directly, but it can send messages to the process that update the state. Another caveat is that a change of state in the process is not propagated to a running async action. An important advantage of this implementation is that the requesting class decides which message is sent to its process when the response returns.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Error handling is important for building reliable systems. Triarc provides a flexible error handling mechanism by delegating error handling to an error handler that you configure.

docs.title: Implementing an Error Handler
docs.text:
To implement an error handler, create a class that implements the Error Handler Interface provided by the framework. The interface requires the class to override Handle Errors.vi with the error handling logic.

Handle Errors.vi receives the error cluster and a Location string that describes where the error occurred. An implementation should:

  • handle both errors and warnings that are passed to it,
  • never pass an error out. The error has been handled when the VI returns,
  • return quickly, because it is called from the process loop of the process that had the error,
  • not log the error. Logging is the job of the log handlers, see Logging Errors.

Typical error handlers show a dialog during testing, ignore selected error codes, or reconnect a device when a known communication error occurs.

docs.title: Error Handling in the Process
docs.text:
The Process class also implements the Error Handler Interface, but delegates the handling of the error to the configured error handler. This means you can call Handle Errors.vi on any process wire to have the error handled.

The Location input of Handle Errors.vi specifies where the error occurred. When an error occurs in Handle Messages.vi of a process, the framework calls Handle Errors.vi with a location that contains the qualified name of the process followed by the message being handled.

The framework also handles errors from helper loops and async handlers of the process. Call Handle Errors.vi yourself in loops that you own and where nobody else would see the error, for example the event loop of a View.vi.

docs.title: Setting an Error Handler
docs.text:
Configure an error handler for a process with Set Error Handler.vi. This works recursively for the processes in an application, regardless of whether a process was added to the application before or after the error handler was configured.

After the error handler has been set, any error passed to Handle Errors.vi is delegated to Handle Errors.vi of the configured error handler. This applies whether the error occurs in the process loop or is passed explicitly on another process wire. An error handler that, for example, displays every error during testing can therefore be replaced by something more appropriate for production.

docs.title: Error Handling in an Application
docs.text:
When Handle Errors.vi of a process is called, the error is delegated to the error handler configured with Set Error Handler.vi. If no error handler has been set for the process, the error is delegated to the context of the process. The error is then passed to the Application that owns the process, and to its configured error handler.

This continues recursively up the process tree, and the first context with a configured error handler handles the error. It is therefore enough to configure the error handler for the top level Application, and all processes in the hierarchy delegate error handling to it. If a process needs different error handling, configure another error handler for that process. This is how you can implement, for example, supervisors.

docs.title: Logging Errors
docs.text: The concepts of error handling and logging are separated in Triarc, and an error handler should in most cases not log errors. Logging should be done by a log handler, because it is often useful to see errors in the context of other log entries. The framework passes errors and warnings to the log handlers of the process, both when they occur in the process loop and when Handle Errors.vi is called explicitly on a process wire. See Logging.

docs.title: Framework Error Codes
docs.text:
The framework uses error codes 9500 to 9515. The error code file is installed with the framework, so the descriptions are shown in the LabVIEW error dialogs.

Code Description 9500 Process not initialized. 9501 Timed out stopping process. 9502 Process was stopped while waiting for request. 9503 Unknown command received. The message was not handled by any class in the hierarchy. 9504 Process cleared while running. 9505 Timed out waiting for request. 9506 Trying to make request to process which is not running. 9507 Request to self is not allowed from inside process loop. 9508 Sending to self should be avoided from inside process loop. 9509 Action not allowed from outside process loop. 9510 Response message not called from within state receiving request or request timed out. 9511 Process already initialized. 9512 Could not find requested process. 9514 Trying to start process which is already running. 9515 The Request caused an error in the process.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Logging gives insight into a running system, both during development and when it is deployed. Most modern programming languages provide the scaffolding for writing log information, but LabVIEW does not. Triarc provides a powerful and flexible logging mechanism.

docs.title: Logging API
docs.text:
The logging API can be used with any Triarc process. It consists of VIs for logging messages with different severity levels.

VI Level Logged when Log Debug.vi DEBUG Only if the conditional disable symbol DEBUG is TRUE for the project. Otherwise the VI does nothing. Log Info.vi INFO Only if there is no error on error in. Log Warning.vi WARNING For unexpected events that the software can recover from. Log Error.vi ERROR Only if there is an error on error in. The error is included in the entry. Log Critical.vi CRITICAL Only if there is an error on error in. Use it for errors that the program may not be able to recover from.

Each entry contains the level, the message and the qualified name of the process that logged it. Logging is not a substitute for error handling: an error that is logged must still be handled.

docs.title: Framework Events
docs.text:
The framework calls the logging API at certain events, such as starting and stopping processes. These events are logged at the INFO level:

  • Started: the process loop has been launched.
  • Running: the process has handled the Start message.
  • Stopped: the process has been asked to stop.
  • Finished: the process loop has finished.

These entries let you see whether errors and other events occur during start-up, execution or shutdown of the process.

The framework passes errors and warnings to the log handlers as they occur, at the ERROR or WARNING level. This applies both to errors in the process loop and to errors passed to Handle Errors.vi explicitly on a process wire outside the loop.

If the DEBUG conditional disable symbol is TRUE, the framework also logs every message sent, received, requested, responded to and broadcast, in the order it happens.

docs.title: Handling Log Messages
docs.text:
What to do with logged messages is up to the user of the framework. The framework delegates the logging to classes that implement the Logging interface, called log handlers. Configure a log handler with Add Log Handler.vi. Several log handlers can be configured at the same time, and every entry is passed to all of them.

Log handlers added to an application apply to all processes in it, recursively, including processes added later. A process without a log handler of its own passes its entries to its context.

docs.title: Implementing a Log Handler
docs.text:
To implement a log handler, create a class that implements the Logging interface. The protected method Log.vi must be overridden to define what to do with an entry. It receives the Level, the Message and the Source of the entry. Common implementations display the log in a text indicator or write it to a file.

The process filters the entries by level before they reach the log handler, so a log handler should log every entry it receives without further filtering. A log handler is called from the process that logs, so it should return quickly. A log handler that writes to a slow medium can be implemented as a process, and its Log.vi can send the entry to that process.

The Coffee Shop example application has a basic log handler.

docs.title: Logging Severity
docs.text:
There are five severity levels. They are available through static VIs in the Logging interface, called Log Debug.vi, Log Info.vi, Log Warning.vi, Log Error.vi, and Log Critical.vi.

The meaning of the levels in a Triarc process is:

  • DEBUG: detailed information for diagnosing problems. Only logged if the DEBUG conditional disable symbol is TRUE.
  • INFO: confirmation that the application is running as expected. If an error occurs upstream of Log Info.vi, nothing is logged.
  • WARNING: something unexpected happened, or a problem may occur soon, but the software still works as expected. The framework logs warnings (an error cluster with status FALSE and a non-zero code) that occur in the process at this level.
  • ERROR: the software could not perform some function. The framework logs errors that occur in the process at this level.
  • CRITICAL: a serious error, indicating that the program itself may be unable to continue running. Logged when called with an upstream error. Not used by the framework.

docs.title: Helper Loops
docs.text: A common pattern in LabVIEW is to use helper loops for periodic tasks. Triarc provides a generic implementation for running helper loops and managing their lifecycle.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: Many tasks need to be done periodically. Examples are a software timed measurement, reading from a buffer, or reconnecting to a network service. In principle this could be solved by sending the same message to the process over and over, but that has drawbacks and timing limitations. A better solution is a helper loop running in parallel to the process.

docs.title: Using a Helper Loop
docs.text:
To add one or more helper loops to a process, make the host process class implement the Helper Loop interface. The interface requires you to override the dynamic dispatch VI Helper Action.vi, which defines the action taken in each iteration of the helper loop. Helper Action.vi is shown below.

When a helper loop is started, Helper Action.vi is called periodically, with the period given by its Loop Period [ms] output. The loop runs until one of the following happens:

  • Helper Action.vi sets Exit? to True,
  • Helper Action.vi returns an error. The error is passed to the error handler of the process, with a location that tells that the helper loop stopped on error,
  • Stop Helper Loops.vi is called,
  • the host process finishes or is cleared.

Warnings returned by Helper Action.vi are logged, and the loop continues.

docs.title: Launching a Helper Loop
docs.text:
To launch a helper loop, call Launch Helper Loop.vi from Handle Messages.vi of the host process. It must be called from inside the process loop. Called from outside, it returns error 9509.

A host process can run many helper loops at the same time. Launch Helper Loop.vi takes a Message string and a Message Data variant, which are passed to Helper Action.vi. Use them to parameterize helper loops and to run different actions in different loops.

The framework stops all helper loops when the process finishes or is cleared. A running helper loop can also be stopped with Stop Helper Loops.vi, shown in the palette above. Note that the VI stops all running helper loops of the process. The framework provides no way to stop helper loops selectively. To stop one loop of several, let Helper Action.vi set Exit? based on its input, or restart the loops that should keep running.

The process broadcasts a Helper Loop message when a helper loop starts, runs and stops.

docs.title: State Data
docs.text:
The class data flows through Helper Action.vi, but it holds a snapshot of the state of the host process from when the helper loop was started. The data in the helper loop is not updated when the state of the host process changes. If the helper loop needs updated data, it must be restarted.

Similarly, the state of the process cannot be changed from within the helper loop. To communicate data back to the host process, call API VIs of the process in Helper Action.vi. The framework makes sure the class data in the helper loop is marked as outside the process loop, so these API VIs send messages to the process.

docs.title: Async Handler
docs.text: Some messages take a long time to handle, and the process should stay responsive while the handling finishes. In such cases an Async Handler is useful: it handles the message asynchronously while the process keeps handling other messages.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
The most direct use case is offloading a blocking or long-running operation, such as file I/O, a network call, or waiting on hardware, so that it does not stall the handling of other messages sent to the process.

Another common use case is handling a message after a delay. Async Action.vi then waits for the delay to elapse and sends the message to the process, which handles it when the delay is over, without blocking the process loop while waiting.

docs.title: Using an Async Handler
docs.text:
To add asynchronous handling to a process, make the host process class implement the Async Handler interface and override Async Action.vi with the action. To launch the action, call Launch Async Handler.vi. It must be called from inside the process loop, typically from Handle Messages.vi. Called from outside, it returns error 9509.

Launch Async Handler.vi takes a Message string and a Message Data variant, which are passed to Async Action.vi. Use them to select between several actions and to pass parameters. Any number of async actions can run at the same time, running the same or different actions.

The example below shows how the Application class launches an async handler to shut down a process.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Async Action.vi runs once per launch, in parallel to the process loop.
  • An error returned by Async Action.vi is passed to the error handler of the process. Errors and warnings are also logged.
  • The process broadcasts an Async Handler message when an async action starts, runs and finishes.
  • The framework does not stop a running async action when the process stops. An action that may run for a long time must stop by itself, for example by watching for the Lifecycle broadcast of the process or by polling Get Lifecycle State.vi.

docs.title: Responding to Requests
docs.text: An async action launched from the case that handles a request can answer the request with Response Message.vi. This keeps the process responsive while a long request is handled; the requester still waits for the response. The action must then respond on every path, and the case must not respond as well. See Responding from an Async Handler.

docs.title: State Data
docs.text:
As for helper loops, the class data in Async Action.vi is a snapshot from when the action was launched. Changes to the state of the process are not seen by a running action, and the action cannot change the state of the process directly. Report results back to the process by calling its API VIs, so that they send messages to the process. Call Leave Process Loop.vi on the class data in Async Action.vi before calling API VIs. The action is launched from inside the process loop, and without this call Get Lifecycle State.vi may still report Handle Message mode, so the API VIs would work on the snapshot instead of sending messages.

Never use the class data in Async Action.vi to access resources that the process loop also uses, such as a driver object. Everything that changes the state of the process should go through messages.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Triarc is developed test first, and processes built on Triarc are designed to be testable. Good test coverage is preferred over debugging: it is much easier to find a problem in a small test case than in a complete application.

docs.title: Testing a Process
docs.text:
A process is tested through its public API, in the same way as it is used in an application:

  1. Initialize the process with Init.vi. Pass a temporary configuration file path, so that the test does not depend on, or change, a real configuration file.
  2. Optionally set a mock error handler and a mock log handler, to observe errors and log entries.
  3. Start the process, call its API VIs, and check the results.
  4. Stop and clear the process.

Requests return values directly, which makes them convenient to test. To test behavior that is only visible as broadcasts, register for the broadcasts of the process in the test before calling the API, and dequeue the broadcasts with a timeout.

Keep the core logic of a process in plain VIs and classes that know nothing about the framework (see Best Practices). That logic can then be tested directly, without starting a process.

docs.title: The Triarc Framework Test Suite
docs.text:
The Triarc Framework Test Suite is installed with the framework. It contains LUnit test case classes that test that a process meets the requirements of the framework. Add it to a project with Tools » Triarc » Add TF Test Suite to Project.

The test case classes form a hierarchy, built on the LUnit test inheritance package:

Test case class Tests Base Test Errors flow through Init.vi and Clear.vi. Clear.vi before Init.vi returns no error. Process Test (inherits Base Test) A configured error handler receives errors. A configured log handler receives log entries. Trigger Broadcast causes a broadcast. View Test (inherits Process Test) View.vi stops when the view is stopped. Showing and hiding the panel causes no errors. Get View VI Reference.vi returns a valid reference. Application Test (inherits Process Test) Runs the inherited process tests on an application. Error Handler Interface Test An error handler handles errors and warnings.

To run these tests on your own class, create a test case class that inherits from the matching test class, and let its Setup.vi provide an instance of the class under test. The inherited tests then run against your class. When a process is created with Tools » Triarc » New Triarc Process, a test class like this is created with it. For a view, it tests the two requirements on View.vi described in View.

Add your own test methods to the same test case class to test the behavior of your process. The protected accessors of the test classes, such as Read Process.vi and Read View.vi, return the object under test, and Get Test Config File Path.vi returns a temporary configuration file path.

docs.title: Test Doubles
docs.text:
The test suite also contains test doubles:

Class Use Mock Error Handler An error handler that records the errors and warnings it receives. Read them with the Spy VIs, for example Spy Wait on Error.vi and Spy Flush Last Error.vi. Mock Log Handler A log handler that records the entries it receives. Read them with Dequeue Log Entry.vi and Flush Spy Queue.vi. Mock Process A process that records the messages it receives and can be told to raise errors, run helper loops and answer requests. It is mainly used to test the framework.

Set the mock error handler with Set Error Handler.vi and the mock log handler with Add Log Handler.vi.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use finite timeouts in tests. A test that waits forever for a broadcast or a request blocks the whole test run.
  • Clear every process a test creates, also when the test fails, so that a failing test does not leave processes running.
  • Do not share state between tests. Triarc has no global state, so tests can create their own processes and handlers without interfering with each other.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Triarc comes with a powerful debugger which enables viewing of messages in an application in real time. The debugger is maintained in its own repository and deployed in a separate VI Package which must be installed in order to use it. The debugger is an invaluable tool, but prefer automated tests over debugging (see Testing).

docs.title: Using the Debugger
docs.text:
To launch the debugger, select Tools » Triarc » Debugger... in LabVIEW. The Debugger window opens. The debugger can also be launched by attaching it to the top level application, as shown below. Attach Debugger.vi is found in the palette under Triarc Debugger. When the debugger is attached, it also shows the broadcasts from the processes in the application.

To enable debugging, the conditional disable symbol DEBUG must be set to TRUE for the project. The symbol can be set directly from the debugger window, with the switch in the lower right corner. Turn debugging off for deployment: it increases the amount of logging done by the framework and adds a slight performance overhead.

docs.title: Process View
docs.text: The Process View shows all active processes, their state and the latest messages they received. Double-click a process to open its Handle Messages.vi, which can then be debugged with the regular LabVIEW debugging tools. If the debugger was attached to the process or its owning application, broadcast messages are also shown.

docs.title: Message View
docs.text: The Message View shows a log of the messages sent in the application, in real time. The list can be filtered by process and by message, and to show, for example, only sent or only received messages. Select a message to see the content of its Message Data variant in the Message Data indicator. Double-click a sent message to open the place it was sent from, and double-click a received message to open the receiving Handle Messages.vi.

docs.title: Debugging without the Debugger
docs.text: With DEBUG set to TRUE, the framework logs every message sent, received, requested, responded to and broadcast at the debug level. A log handler that writes to a file or a text indicator then gives a trace of the communication in the application. See Logging.

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
Configuration management is needed in most software systems, and test systems are no exception, quite the contrary. Parameters that should be editable after the system has been built and deployed are best kept outside the source code. Because configuration management is so central to test systems, the Triarc Framework provides a framework for it.

Configurations can be stored in any format. A common choice is human readable text files. LabVIEW comes with built in functions for key-value pairs in Windows style .ini files. Other common choices are the Windows registry or a database.

docs.title: Triarc Configuration Interface
docs.text: The Configuration interface defines abstract methods for reading and writing configuration data. An implementation can use any storage technology. This is useful, for example, for an in-memory implementation used in tests, or for an object that carries configuration data.

docs.title: Triarc Configuration File Interface
docs.text:
A common way to store configurations is in human readable text files. This works well in many cases, and text files are easy to manage and version control.

The Configuration File interface implements the Configuration interface with an ini file. To make a class configurable, let it implement Configuration File. The class must inherit from Base, which holds the file path and the file reference. The API is shown in the test case below, where configurations are written to a text file.

VI Description Read Boolean.vi, Read Double.vi, Read I32.vi, Read U32.vi, Read String.vi, Read Path.vi Read the value of a key. If the key is missing, the default value is written to the file and returned. Read Comma Separated String.vi Reads a string and splits it at commas into an array of trimmed strings. Write Boolean.vi, Write Double.vi, Write I32.vi, Write U32.vi, Write String.vi, Write Path.vi Write the value of a key. Get All Keys.vi Returns the names of all keys in the section of the object. Open Config.vi, Close Config.vi Open and close the file around many reads. Optional.

The keys are read from and written to the section of the object. For a process, the section is named after its qualified name, for example [Main::Motion::Source]. For a Base object that is not a process, the section is named after its name.

docs.title: The Configuration File
docs.text: The configuration file path is an optional input of Init.vi. If no path is given, a default path is used. Read Config File Path.vi returns the path in use. In the development environment on Windows, the default is Config\Config.ini in the application directory, which is the folder of the LabVIEW project. In a built Windows application, the default is under the local application data folder of the user, in a folder named after the company and product of the executable. On NI Linux Real-Time, the default is /home/lvuser/natinst/bin/config/config.ini. If the file does not exist, it is created, together with the folders containing it.

docs.title: Reading the Configuration of a Process
docs.text:
Override the protected Read Configuration.vi of the process to read its configuration. The framework calls it in the process loop when the process handles the Init message, the first message handled when it starts. Store the values directly in the class data: Read Configuration.vi runs in the process loop, where the class data may be accessed.

An Application can also create and add its processes in Read Configuration.vi, for example reading the names of the processes to create from a key in its own section.

docs.title: Thread Safety
docs.text:
The Configuration File API is designed to be thread safe and optimized for reading. Many processes can read from and write to the same configuration file without race conditions. This is done by allowing only one process at a time to write to the configuration file.

If many keys are read in sequence, use Open Config.vi and Close Config.vi, as shown below. This avoids the overhead of opening and closing the file for each read. Without Open Config.vi, each read opens and closes the file itself.

docs.title: Practices and Antipatterns
docs.text: There are a few pitfalls to be aware of when working with configurations, and they are often overlooked. This section assumes that configurations are stored in a file, but the same applies to any storage technology.

docs.title: Configuration Data is Global
docs.text:
As configurations are stored in one or more text files, any part of the application that can find and parse the file can access the configuration information. This means there is an inherent risk of race conditions, and care should be taken whenever a configuration is updated.

In TF, the configuration functions make sure that each process can only access its own section of the configuration file. This reduces the risk of race conditions.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text: If a file is opened for writing in several places at the same time, race conditions can occur. The process that closes the file last overwrites the changes that others made since it opened the file. TF prevents this with synchronization that allows only a single process at a time to open the file for writing.

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text:
If a key is not found, the native LabVIEW configuration file functions return a default value set by the developer. If a key is, for example, misspelled in the file, the user of the system gets no feedback on what the system expects, which can cause a lot of pain.

To mitigate this, TF writes the default value to the configuration file when a key is not found. Missing keys are thereby added to the file, and if the whole file is missing, a file with the default configuration is created. A key that is missing from a configuration file is therefore not an error. Make sure the default value wired to each read is sensible: an unwired default is the default of the data type, for example 0 or an empty string.

docs.title: Lack of Structure
docs.text:
With the native LabVIEW configuration file functions, the developer is responsible for using reasonable sections when saving configuration data. This often leads to a structure that degrades over time as more fields are added.

TF enforces a structure on the configuration file, because each process has its own section. If, for example, two instances of a process control two hardware devices, each instance has its own section named after the process. The two devices can then be configured independently, and the only thing the developer needs to do is give the processes unique names.

docs.title: Don't Marry the Framework
docs.text: Triarc should make building your application easier, not become a dependency your domain logic cannot live without. Keep the actual business logic - algorithms, calculations, domain rules - in plain VIs and classes that know nothing about Process, View, or messaging. Let the Process and View act as a thin integration layer that calls into this core logic. This keeps the core logic portable, easy to reuse outside the framework, and cheap to test in isolation.

docs.title: A good Process is an Idle Process
docs.text: To ensure responsiveness of the system, processes should spend most of their time waiting for messages. To enable this, heavy processing should be dispatched into a Helper Loop and operations waiting with a long timeout should be handled by an Async Action.

docs.title: Avoid sending messages to self
docs.text: It can be tempting to have a process send a message to itself, for example to break up a long operation into steps or to re-trigger its own logic. This should be avoided, since there is no guarantee that other, externally sent messages will not be interleaved between the self-sent message and its handling. Relying on a process sending itself messages breaks the assumption that each message is handled atomically and makes the resulting behavior harder to reason about and test. Model repeating or multi-step behavior using process state and Helper Loops instead.

docs.title: Use helper loops for repetitive tasks
docs.text: Periodic work, such as polling a buffer, taking a software timed measurement, or retrying a connection, should not be implemented by having a process repeatedly re-send a message to itself. Doing so has drawbacks and timing limitations, since it competes with normal messaging traffic and its timing is only as reliable as the process loop. Instead, use a Helper Loop, which runs the periodic action in parallel to the process on its own configurable period.

docs.title: Use async handler for blocking tasks
docs.text: Any operation that may block or take a significant amount of time, such as file I/O, network calls, or waiting on hardware, should not be run directly in the process loop. Doing so stalls the handling of every other message sent to the process for as long as the operation takes. Use an Async Handler to run the operation on a separate thread while the process remains responsive, and be notified of the result via messaging once it completes.

docs.title: Separate core from framework
docs.text: Structure applications so that framework-specific code (message handlers, view wiring, lifecycle management) is kept separate from the core logic it delegates to. This makes it possible to unit test the core logic directly, without needing a running process, and keeps Handle Messages.vi implementations focused on dispatching rather than doing the actual work. It also means core logic can be reused in a different context or migrated to a different framework with minimal changes.

docs.title: Only touch the class data in the process loop
docs.text: The class data of a process is only valid in the process loop, that is in Handle Messages.vi and the VIs it calls. Never unbundle or bundle the class data in View.vi, Helper Action.vi, Async Action.vi, or in code that uses the process from outside. Use API VIs instead, and let the process change its own state when it handles the message.

docs.title: One API VI per message
docs.text: Wrap every message in an API VI that hard codes the message string and has typed inputs and outputs. Use the tools in the right-click menu of the process class, Generate API VI..., Generate Getter... and Generate Setter..., to create them. When you rename a message, rename both the string in the API VI and the case in Handle Messages.vi.

docs.title: Always respond to requests
docs.text: The case that handles a request must call Response Message.vi on every path, including the error paths. Otherwise the requester waits until its timeout expires. If the case hands the work to an async action, the action must respond on every path instead, and the case must not respond as well. Give requests a timeout that is longer than the worst-case time to handle them, and avoid infinite timeouts for requests that involve hardware.

docs.title: Prefer broadcasts over requests from views
docs.text: A view that requests data from its process blocks while it waits. Let the process broadcast its state when it changes, and handle Trigger Broadcast by broadcasting the current state, so that a new view can ask for the state once and then follow the broadcasts.

docs.title: Configure handlers once, at the top
docs.text: Set the error handler and add the log handlers on the top level application. They apply to every process in the application, including processes added later. Configure a separate error handler on a process only when that process needs different error handling.

docs.title: Name processes uniquely
docs.text: Processes owned by the same application must have unique names. The qualified name of a process is used as the name of its configuration section, the location of its errors and the source of its log entries, so choose names that are meaningful to someone reading a configuration file or a log.

docs.title: Design Discussion
docs.text: When designing the Triarc Framework, one of the goals was approachability and ease of use while retaining the full power of the actor model. Software design is always about making trade offs, and in order to make the readability higher some trade offs have been made. This document discusses the most important of these.

docs.title: Values and Design Principles
docs.text: The core values and design principles employed by TF are discussed in this section.

docs.title: Let the data flow
docs.text: The concept of data flow is one of the key strengths of LabVIEW and should be embraced. Passing data by value is to prefer as default, over passing data by reference.

docs.title: Processing in the Process
docs.text: All major processing should take place within the process. This makes API calls fast and reliable, while protecting the consistency of the process state.

docs.title: Messaging
docs.text: Information is exchanged between processes using asynchronous messaging. All messages have equal priority, to reduce unnecessary complexity. The handling of each message should be atomic, i.e. should not be spread out over multiple states.

docs.title: No Global Mutable State
docs.text: By avoiding any kind of global mutable state, applications become more robust and easier to understand and reason about. It is also a prerequisite for effective testing, as tests would interfere if they were to share global resources. This means that global variables, functional global variables (FGVs), named queues, etc. are prohibited.
